section.title: A first map of the book

introduction.p: Slope measures a rate of change, and signed area measures an accumulated change. Finite differences and finite sums give discrete versions of these operations. Limits will connect them to derivatives and integrals.

subsection.title: Derivative: from position to velocity
subsection.p: The derivative is the precise version of instantaneous rate of change.
Starting with signed position s(t), the derivative answers:

p.me: \text{How fast is }s(t)\text{ changing at this instant?}

The derivative is local. It studies what happens near one input a. On a graph, it gives the slope of the tangent line. In motion, it gives velocity. In an applied model, it gives sensitivity: how much the output changes when the input is nudged.

subsection.title: Integral: from velocity to position
subsection.p: The integral is the precise version of accumulated signed change.
Starting with velocity v(t), the integral answers:

p.me: \text{How much signed position has accumulated over an interval?}

subsection.p: The notation will be
This means the signed accumulation of v(t) from t=a to t=b. If v(t) is above the time axis, it contributes positively. If v(t) is below the time axis, it contributes negatively.

The integral is global. It uses the whole interval, not just one instant. On a graph, it is signed area. In motion, it is displacement. In applications, it can represent accumulated mass, work, energy, probability, cost, or growth.

Approximation is not a temporary trick before the exact answer arrives. In science, engineering, economics, and computation, approximation is often the answer we can actually use. The real question is:

subsection.title: Differential equations: when the law gives the derivative
subsection.p: Sometimes a problem does not give the function directly. It gives a law for how the function changes.
For example, a population P(t) might grow at a rate proportional to its current size:
This equation does not tell us P(t) outright. It tells us the derivative of P. To solve the problem, we must find a function whose rate of change behaves in the required way.
A cooling cup of coffee can be modeled by
The farther the coffee temperature is from room temperature, the faster it cools. Again, the law is written in the language of derivatives.
Equations involving derivatives are called differential equations. They are one of the main reasons calculus became the language of science.

exercise.title: Where do derivative, integral, approximation, and differential equations sit on the map?

statement.p: Explain the roles of derivatives, integrals, approximations, and differential equations in describing motion. Give one question answered by each.

hint.p: Derivative extracts a rate. Integral accumulates a rate. Approximation is what we do when an exact formula is unavailable. A differential equation is a law that hands us the rate directly.

subsection.title: The road in one picture

figure.caption: The main ideas of the book are connected from the beginning. The derivative measures local change. The integral accumulates change. Approximation makes both useful. Differential equations express laws in the language of change.

subsection.p: This map is only a beginning. Two phrases still need a careful foundation: h\to0 and \text{better and better approximations by sums}.
Both processes require a precise meaning of approximation error and nearness. The next chapters define distances, intervals, functions, and limits.

exercise.title: Why is nearness the hidden idea behind the whole map?

statement.p: What must be specified to make h\to0 and convergence of approximating sums precise? Explain the input or index, the quantity being approximated, and the allowed error.

hint.p: You need a way to say that one number can be forced as close as you like to another by making an input close enough. That is the job of limits, after a language for distance on the line.
